Joram
jō'răm
n. (contracted form of Jehoram, borne by contemporary kings of Israel and Judah — the son of Ahab who half-reformed, and the son of Jehoshaphat who murdered his brothers)
From Hebrew Yoram, a contraction of Yehoram, “the LORD is exalted”, from Yah and rum, to be high. The KJV uses Joram and Jehoram interchangeably, sometimes of the same man in the same chapter.

Biblical Definition

Joram is the shortened form of Jehoram, and two kings of that name reigned at the same time on either side of the border, married into one another's houses. Joram son of Ahab ruled Israel twelve years, and the Chronicler's verdict on him is unusually qualified: “he wrought evil in the sight of the LORD; but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made” (2Ki 3:2). He kept the calves of Jeroboam, and half-reform is what the phrase “but not like his father” is for. Most of Elisha's public ministry falls in his reign. He was killed by Jehu with an arrow between the shoulders, and his body cast into the plot of Naboth the Jezreelite (2Ki 9:24) — the field where the judgment on Ahab's house had been pronounced. Jehoram of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, began to reign in his fifth year (2Ki 8:16), married Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, slew all his brethren with the sword, and “walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab” (2Ki 8:18). He received a writing from Elijah, died of an incurable disease of the bowels, and departed “without being desired”. Two Jorams, one alliance, and a name meaning “the LORD is exalted” over both.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Joram; in sacred history it is a contraction of Jehoram, borne by a king of Israel, the son of Ahab, and a king of Judah, the son of Jehoshaphat.

expand to see more

JORAM, n. A contracted form of Jehoram, signifying the Lord is exalted.

Joram the son of Ahab reigned twelve years over Israel, and put away the image of Baal, but cleaved to the sins of Jeroboam.

He warred with Moab and with Syria, and was slain by Jehu in the portion of Naboth the Jezreelite.

Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat reigned eight years over Judah, and slew all his brethren with the sword.

He married the daughter of Ahab, and died of a sore disease, and departed without being desired.

Key Scripture

2Ki 3:2 — "And he wrought evil in the sight of the LORD; but not like his father, and like his mother: for he put away the image of Baal that his father had made."

2Ki 8:16 — "And in the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign."

2Ki 8:18 — "And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab: for the daughter of Ahab was his wife: and he did evil in the sight of the LORD."

2Ki 9:24 — "And Jehu drew a bow with his full strength, and smote Jehoram between his arms, and the arrow went out at his heart, and he sunk down in his chariot."

Modern Corruption

Partial reformation is graded as progress; Scripture grades it as evil qualified, and the calves Joram kept destroyed the kingdom the Baal-image he removed had not.

expand to see more

2Ki 3:2 is the classic text on half-measures. Joram removed the most conspicuous idol in the land — his father's image of Baal, the very thing Elijah had contended against on Carmel — and the Spirit of God records it, and still says he wrought evil. He kept Jeroboam's calves, which were not a foreign god at all but a convenient way of worshipping the true God: the LORD, at Bethel and Dan, in a form Israel had chosen. That is the sin the northern kingdom died of, and it is far more durable than open paganism because it wears the right name. The regulative principle of worship is the church's protection here: what God has not commanded in His worship is not permitted, however sincerely it is offered to Him.

The second corruption is the alliance itself. Jehoshaphat was a good king who made one persistent mistake — he married his son to Ahab's daughter for the sake of national unity. The fruit of it was Jehoram murdering his brothers, Athaliah nearly extinguishing the line of David, and two generations of Baal worship in Jerusalem. The seer Jehu had asked Jehoshaphat the question directly: “Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?” (2Ch 19:2). Good men make dynastic bargains with evil houses for reasons that look like prudence, and their grandchildren pay.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yoram (H3141) and Yehoram (H3088), from Yah (H3050) and rum (H7311), to be exalted.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yehoram (H3088) — Jehoram, “the LORD is exalted”; the full form of the name.

Hebrew Yoram (H3141) — Joram; the contraction, used of the same men interchangeably.

Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to be lifted up; the root of the theophoric element.

Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing image or pillar; the Baal-image Joram removed (2Ki 3:2).

Hebrew chelqah (H2513) — a portion of ground; Naboth's plot, where Joram's body was cast (2Ki 9:25-26).

Usage

"“But not like his father, and like his mother” — reform measured and found short."

"“The daughter of Ahab was his wife” — the marriage that poisoned Judah."

"“Smote Jehoram between his arms” — judgment overtaking a house in Naboth's field."
